title: Projects and Publications
text:
Beyond tracing the past: Modelling and representing rock art
Editors: Oliver Vogels, Paolo Medici, Ashely Green, Eymard Fäder, Rebecca Döhl
Call for papers: October 2026 - July 2027
The context for the formation and use of visual communication systems, such as rock art (including petroglyphs and paintings), wall art, or graffiti, is mainly analysed through formal methods of interpretation (Taçon and Chippindale, 1998). During the last decade these formal methods shifted more to digital and computational methods, comprising a wide range of approaches, applications, and techniques (Carrero-Pazos et al., 2022; Valdez-Tullett and Figueiredo Persson, 2023). These methods cover well-established GIS-centred analysis of the spatial context of rock art, computational analysis of rock art production, and extended reality (XR) applications for cultural heritage and engagement. On both the local- and large-scale, digital and computational methods play an important role in understanding visual communication systems and the people that created them. Incorporating digital methods in rock art research creates frameworks for the analysis of creation, meaning, and exchange of visual communication systems.
To highlight the people behind the visual communication, this volume aims to explore all aspects of social engagement with rock art from its creation to its consumption and the feedback within these processes. While we refer to rock art as a prime example of visual communication, we embrace all expressions of semantic visuality, such as graffiti, visual marking systems, and wall art. We welcome contributions on methods, new insights and results from digital methods, and dissemination around the human-centred lifecycle of historic and prehistoric rock art. Broadly, topics can include, but are not limited to:

new approaches in digital visualisation methods
success and failure of AI-supported methods in rock art documentation and analysis
new computational approaches to rock art analysis, contextualisation, and visualisation
discussions of theoretical and methodological frameworks for digital rock art research

References
Carrero-Pazos, M., Döhl, R., Rensburg, J.J. van, Medici, P., Vázquez-Martínez, A., 2022. Rock Art Research in the Digital Era: Case Studies from the 20th International Rock Art Congress IFRAO 2018, Valcamonica (Italy), Rock Art Research in the Digital Era: Case Studies from the 20th International Rock Art Congress IFRAO 2018, Valcamonica (Italy). DOI: 10.30861/9781407360119
Taçon, P.S.C., Chippindale, C., 1998. An Archaeology of Rock-Art Through Informed Methods and Formal Methods, in: Chippindale, C. (Ed.), The Archaeology of Rock-Art. Cambridge Univ. Press, Cambridge, pp. 1–10.
Valdez-Tullett, J., Figueiredo Persson, S., 2023. Digital Rock Art: Beyond “Pretty Pictures.” F1000Research 12, 523. DOI: 10.12688/f1000research.127249.1


Please visit https://journal.caa-international.org/special-collections for further information about CAA Special Collections, article publication charges, peer-review system, and submission guidelines.

title: About
text:
Prehistoric art tells us about past people from their own perspectives. As such, past artistic expressions should not be underestimated as both an archaeological source and cultural heritage. Over the last few decades, research on rock art, as well as other forms of artistic expression in ancient societies, such as epigraphy and the study of wall paintings, has increasingly shifted towards digital and computational methods. These methods comprise a wide range of approaches and techniques along with their respective theoretical considerations. Methods include well-established geospatial analysis of rock art contexts, computational and quantitative analysis (including AI approaches) of rock art production, and extended reality (XR) applications for cultural heritage and engagement. On both the local and the large scale, digital and computational methods play an important role in understanding rock art today.
Rock art is widely understood as a communication system deeply rooted in the respective worldview of its creators. In other words, rock art is ‘symbolically encoded’. The use, function, meaning, or contexts of rock art are therefore not directly accessible to cultures who do not share the same symbolic system.

title: About
text:
Aims and Objectives
The Digital Rock Art Research Special Interest Group (SIG-DRAR) aims to enable the development of new digital workflows for documentation, analysis, conservation, and data sharing that improve our understanding of the creation, consumption, and management of prehistoric art art worldwide. Within this, we would particularly like to explore:

best-practice workflows in digital rock art documentation - from individual sites to digital publication
how to improve relative and absolute chronology methods
how to improve the use of spatial, statistical, and chronological methods in the analysis of rock art
how to better understand the spatial, social and functional context of rock art
how to better understand human and natural effects on rock art and cultural heritage sites
how to improve management and conservation of rock art sites with digital methods
how to include local communities in documentation, preservation and management with digital tools
how to not rest our understanding and interpretation of prehistoric art on preconceptions of our present-day societies

The SIG’s long-term goal is to gain a better understanding of past and present processes related to the production and consumption of rock art and improved methods in rock art research.

title: About
text:
Activities
To achieve these goals, the SIG will:

Establish a network of rock art researchers using computational or quantitative methods in rock art research for knowledge exchange
Run sessions at CAA conferences more regularly (at least every 2 years)
Advance digital and computer-aided methods in rock art research
Include theoretical frameworks in digital documentation and analysis of rock art
Enable researchers (from other archaeology subdisciplines) to adequately document rock art
Highlight rock art as valuable cultural heritage assets
Host (digital) meetings with the SIG members and other interested parties

title: Digital Rock Art Research
text:
This CAA International Special Interest Group (SIG) on Digital Rock Art Research focuses on enabling the development of digital workflows for documentation, analysis, conservation, and data sharing that improve our understanding of the creation, consumption, and management of rock art worldwide.
We are inclusive of all types of prehistoric art, regardless of its chronology, geography, technique, or cultural context.
Interested in joining? Please contact us via email or take a look at the SIG Coordinators.




SIG Members have co-organised a session at the Kiel Conference 2027 (Paper submissions closed) (see Events)
JCAA Special Collection on digital rock art research (see the Call for Papers)




After a workshop on digital rock art research in Berlin (2023) and great discussion within sessions at CAA 2025 in Athens and CAA 2026 in Vienna, we decided to propose a CAA Special Interest Group on digital rock art research. The SIG was approved in 2026 at CAA Vienna.
